Thus, the roots of the original equation coincide with the roots of the equation

$$

\sin 3 x \cdot \sin \frac{5}{2} x=0

After removing the stencil, the encrypted message appears on the sheet of paper.

5. Solve the equation $x^{2}-x y-6 y^{2}+2 x+19 y=18$ in integers.

Rewrite the equation as

$$
x^{2}-x(y-2)-6 y^{2}+19 y+k=18+k
$$

and we will choose the number $k$ so that the discriminant of the quadratic trinomial on the left side of the equation becomes a perfect square. We have

$$
D=25 y^{2}-80 y+4-4 k
$$

To obtain a perfect square, we need $k=-15$. Now we have the opportunity to factor the left side of our equation

$$
x_{1,2}=\frac{y-2 \pm(5 y-8)}{2} \Rightarrow(x-3 y+5)(x+2 y-3)=3
$$

The factors on the left side are integers, so we get four systems

$$
\left\{\begin{array}{l}
x-3 y+5=1 \\
x+2 y-3=3
\end{array},\left\{\begin{array}{l}
x-3 y+5=-1 \\
x+2 y-3=-3
\end{array},\left\{\begin{array}{l}
x-3 y+5=3 \\
x+2 y-3=1
\end{array},\left\{\begin{array}{l}
x-3 y+5=-3 \\
x+2 y-3=-1
\end{array}\right.\right.\right.\right.
$$

Solve these systems and we get the answer.

In a domino game with the numbers \(0,1,2, \ldots, 6\), each tile is divided into two halves, each half bearing one of the numbers.

In a domino game, all combinations of two of the numbers 0, 1, 2, .. , 6 occur exactly once.

A chain is formed when several tiles are placed next to each other in a sequence such that adjacent halves of neighboring tiles always bear the same number.

A chain is called closed if the two tile halves at the free ends of the chain also bear the same number.

A closed chain of three different tiles is briefly called a triplet chain. Two triplet chains are considered the same if and only if they consist of the same tiles.

Determine the number of all sets \(\left\{K_{1}, \ldots, K_{7}\right\}\) consisting of exactly 7 different triplet chains \(K_{1}, \ldots, K_{7}\), where each tile of the domino game appears in at most one of the chains \(K_{1}, \ldots, K_{7}\)!

(As usual, two sets \(\mathrm{M}=\left\{K_{1}, \ldots, K_{7}\right\}\) and \(M^{\prime}=\left\{K_{1}^{\prime}, \ldots, K_{7}^{\prime}\right\}\) are considered equal if and only if every chain \(K_{i}\) contained in the set \(M\) is also contained in \(M^{\prime}\) and vice versa every chain contained in \(M^{\prime}\) is also contained in \(M\).)

What is the largest number of distinct palindromic subsequences that such a sequence of length $n$ can contain?

From the conditions given in the problem, we know that there exists an odd cycle in the graph. Since the number of points is finite, by the extreme principle, we know that there must exist the shortest odd cycle $A_{1} A_{2} \cdots A_{2 k+1} A_{1}$. Furthermore, in the shortest odd cycle, any two points $A_{i}$ and $A_{j}(j \neq i \pm 1)$ must not be connected, thus the internal structure of the odd cycle is fully understood. At this point, starting from the shortest odd cycle $C$, the entire graph can be divided into two parts: one part is the odd cycle $A_{1} A_{2} \cdots A_{2 k+1} A_{1}$, and the other part is all the points except $A_{1} A_{2} \cdots A_{2 k+1} A_{1}$. We only need to understand the structure of each part and the connection situation between the two parts to grasp the overall structure.
